prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made possible incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part B049 prize with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and the reasons are scientific. The discovery is a physiological principle: a gut hormone whose glucose-dependent action on insulin secretion, together with its effects on appetite and gastric emptying, was defined in humans, placed in the proglucagon peptide system, and tied to the active truncated peptide. It has been confirmed independently for decades. Randomized trials now show benefit for glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes, so the arc from mechanism to medicine is complete and the maturity question does not arise. The chair's question on framing matters to me. I would keep the citation on the physiology and the active form and let the therapies appear as the consequence. That keeps the prize on a discovery, and it applies the same standard I would apply to CAR-T and imatinib, where I would also look for the discovery that opened the field before the product that reached the clinic. Nothing in round 1 moved me towards a second part. Six names would have to be squeezed into three, and every second part I can think of damages either the GLP-1 attribution or the second achievement.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weak point, and round 1 did not remove it. The third seat is a judgment between Mojsov and Knudsen, and Habener sits outside the credited names even though several of us regard his proglucagon and GLP-1 work as part of the story. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is described by all six of us as disputed, and none of us has verified it from primary documents. If I am wrong that this is a dispute of degree and not of substance, the trio is weaker. A physiology-centred prize can also be read as skipping the drug that changed practice, which is Sandberg's strongest argument. Finally, long-term safety and durability of the therapies are still accumulating. I do not think that affects the discovery case, but it bears on how confidently the citation can speak about the therapies.

responses.point: Sandberg keeps Knudsen in the third seat on the ground that acylation-based half-life extension was a conceptually new step, and that the Mojsov priority claim is the one most entangled with Habener's group.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my configuration and I have weighed it again. I accept that her priority claim is the more entangled one, and that is a real risk. But I still read acylation as optimization of a mechanism that already existed. The step that made any analogue meaningful was identifying which peptide form is active, and Mojsov is tied to that step. I also doubt that a priority dispute of degree should remove her while leaving the discovery in place. I have not changed my position, and I stay with the condition I gave in round 1: if the committee decides that the citation must explicitly cover translation into drugs, Knudsen should replace Mojsov, because a four-name arc does not fit in three. On the chair's last question, I did not raise any conduct concern about a credited person on TOR. My round-1 statement had no such point, so I cannot clarify it from my own evidence. I would set it aside unless someone brings documentation.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks for a consistent discovery-versus-development standard across GLP-1, imatinib and CAR-T, and questions whether a prize this popular is being tested as hard as the others.
responses.response: I agree that we should state the standard and apply it to every candidate. Mine is to credit the finding that opened the field. That finding can be a physiological principle, a mechanism or a molecular entity, and the clinical proof is the consequence. On that standard GLP-1 holds because Holst, Drucker and Mojsov each have a discovery step of their own. I am less sure the same standard carries imatinib and CAR-T cleanly. For imatinib the BCR-ABL kinase biology belongs partly to others, and for CAR-T the receptor concept is Eshhar's. On your wider worry, I tested the GLP-1 trio against the strongest objection I could build, which is Knudsen, and it survived on the discovery standard. It would not survive if we dropped that standard, and I think we should say that openly.

responses.point: Linnarsson says the Eshhar gap narrows the CAR-T citation to the clinical and costimulatory advances, so B014 is the strongest alternative but not a co-equal second part.
responses.response: I agree, and it moves me further than in round 1. The June and Sadelain pair is right on the engineering, but a citation worded around costimulated receptors and clinical translation is a narrower achievement than the title suggests, and I do not think wording solves the omission of Eshhar. That is why B014 stays my first alternative and is not a second part. A second part would also force a cut inside the GLP-1 trio, and I would not trade a clean physiological attribution for a contested one. I do disagree with one thing. Linnarsson treats Mojsov's seat as a place where we could simply swap in Knudsen. I would swap only if the citation changes, not because a name looks safer.

responses.point: Perlmann wants the Mojsov priority question settled first, and he argued that if no trio of optogenetics names excludes no central contributor, that is a reason not to put it at the top this year.
responses.response: On optogenetics I now agree with you more than I did in round 1. My earlier trio of Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann tried to cover the molecular discovery and the neuronal demonstration in three names, and your reply showed that it does so by making a choice I cannot defend from the documents. Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck each have a claim comparable to the names I picked. So B021 remains an alternative and not a preferred part. On Mojsov, I cannot give you what you ask for. I have no verified primary documents on the early GLP-1 papers and I am working from recollection, as I said in round 1. What I can offer is the structure of the judgment. If the priority dispute is one of degree, as Svenningsson argues, Mojsov stays. If the primary literature showed that the active-form identification belongs mainly to Habener's group, then the credit would have to change, and I would want the committee to check this before the vote and not rely on any of our memories.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active truncated GLP-1 holds up against the primary literature, including Habener's group. I have not verified it, and I do not think anyone on the committee has.
Whether the committee will word the citation on physiology and the active form only, or also on the long-acting therapies. This decides between Mojsov and Knudsen.
Whether any trio for optogenetics can avoid excluding a central contributor. I now doubt it.
Whether the Eshhar omission can be handled in a CAR-T citation, which matters only if the committee turns to B014.
Long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy, which are still accumulating.
statement.conflict_note: I have no conflict with any credited candidate on the shortlist. My documented connections (a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, work with Patrik Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann) do not involve any credited name. I work on motor circuits and have a scientific interest in optogenetics as a tool, but no documented personal tie to Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth, Hegemann, Miesenboeck or Nagel, and optogenetics is not in my preferred configuration. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
